title: How passwords actually leak
body_md:
## A leak is only the first link

On a weekday evening an email arrives from a model-railway forum you joined years ago: its database has been copied. Your stomach drops. It helps to notice how much still has to happen before a stranger is sitting in your inbox. A leaked address is not a leaked password, and a leaked password is not yet a login. Each is a separate link, and the job is to find out which links are yours to break: which secret was exposed, where else you used it, and whether any account still has a live session or a recovery route an intruder could use. Not every breach contains readable passwords, and not every stolen hash gives way quickly.

### Four ways in

When a service is breached, the loot varies. It might be email addresses, password hashes, plaintext passwords or other data, and sometimes no passwords at all. A hash is a one-way fingerprint of a password, kept so the service can check what you type without storing the password itself. How well it stands up to offline guessing depends on the password you chose and on how carefully the service hashed it.

The other routes skip the service altogether. Malware on your own device can capture credentials as you type them, or session data once you are signed in. A fake sign-in page collects whatever you enter, sometimes a one-time code as well. And attackers can take an email-and-password pair from one leak and try it on other services. That is **credential stuffing**, and it works only where the password was reused.

A unique generated password keeps one site’s leak inside that site. It does nothing about a hijacked session or an infected device. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a separate hurdle, though a code you type by hand can be relayed through a live phishing page while you wait. Passkeys and properly set-up FIDO security keys resist that relay, because they tie the sign-in to the service’s real domain.

### From breach notice to to-do list

Open the affected service from a saved bookmark or by typing its address yourself, never through the sign-in button in the notification. Read the service’s own account of the incident: what data was involved, when, and what it asks you to do. If the provider says your password was exposed, or you suspect it was, change it. If you used that password anywhere else, change every copy, starting with your primary email and your financial accounts. Then look at sessions, recovery methods and MFA on any account an intruder might have reached. If malware on your device is plausible, clean the device before you type a fresh secret into it.

Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) can tell you whether an address appears in the incidents it has indexed. It does **not** tell you which password went with that address, and an empty result is not proof of safety. Never type a real password into this lesson or into a breach-checking site you found by chance. To check your passwords, use your password manager’s own health check, and read the official HIBP documentation to see how such checks work.

widget_config.goal: Trace a reported exposure to the accounts that need action, without treating a listed email address as proof that a password was stolen.
widget_config.today_action: Find one old breach notice and read it on the provider’s own site. List every place you reused that password, then replace each one from an account page you opened yourself.
widget_config.scope: General education that applies across countries; breach details and account controls depend on the provider. The cases are invented. Sources checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.scope: The service’s own documentation. A listed address does not prove its password leaked, and coverage is incomplete.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authenticators
sources.scope: US federal technical standard for digital identity; covers phishing resistance and types of authenticator.

sources.title: FTC: How To Recover Your Hacked Email or Social Media Account
sources.scope: US consumer guidance; controls differ by provider.

blocks.title: A forum password reused at a payment service
blocks.situation: A forum for vintage-synth owners posts a notice: password hashes were stolen. One member, who used the same password for a payment account, shrugs: the payment service has reported nothing.
blocks.analysis: That hash may never be cracked, but you cannot count on that: reuse is what links the two accounts. Replace the payment password first, then the forum one, check the payment account’s sessions and switch on the strongest MFA it offers. Do not wait for proof of misuse.

blocks.title: A genuine notice that names only email addresses
blocks.situation: A public library sends a genuine incident notice: email addresses and reading preferences were exposed, and passwords were not in the affected system.
blocks.analysis: This still matters for privacy, and it can feed targeted phishing, but it is no evidence that a password leaked. Confirm the notice on the library’s own site, expect impersonators to follow up, and skip the sweeping password reset unless other evidence turns up.

blocks.title: When a small forum is breached
blocks.setup: An invented scenario. A craft forum reports that hashes were stolen. You once reused its password for an email account and a shop, and you are working on a device you trust.

steps.prompt: A message arrives with a link to “check your password.” Where do you start?

choices.text: Type your password into the checker in the message.
choices.consequence: The page now holds a secret that opens real accounts.
choices.explanation: A breach warning is easy to copy or forge. Never hand a real password to a page you cannot vouch for.

choices.text: Go to the forum by a saved route and read what it says about the incident.
choices.consequence: You learn which kinds of data were taken, and the message never gets a sign-in from you.
choices.explanation: A page you opened yourself shows what was actually reported. The link in the message is not needed for that.

steps.prompt: The forum says hashes may be exposed, and that old password also protects your email. Which change comes first?

choices.text: Replace the email password with a unique one and check the email account’s MFA.
choices.consequence: The most damaging reuse route closes.
choices.explanation: Email usually receives the reset links for other accounts, so priority follows what an intruder could reach.

choices.text: Change only the forum password and wait for alerts from your email provider.
choices.consequence: If the hash is cracked, the email password still works.
choices.explanation: Resetting a password at the forum does nothing to the same password anywhere else.

steps.prompt: In your email you spot a session you do not recognise. What now?

choices.text: Ignore it; the new password will have logged everyone out.
choices.consequence: The session may still be live.
choices.explanation: Whether a password change ends sessions depends on the service, so check the real settings.

choices.text: Sign it out in security settings, check recovery details and forwarding, then change the secrets it could have reached.
choices.consequence: You close the open route and the places an intruder might hide.
choices.explanation: A password change on its own can leave a live session or a malicious forwarding rule behind.

steps.prompt: HIBP finds nothing for your second address. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Nothing definite. Keep unique passwords and MFA on that address.
choices.consequence: You do not mistake a gap in the index for a clean bill of health.
choices.explanation: HIBP covers the incidents it has indexed, not every exposure and not malware on a device.

choices.text: That address has never been exposed anywhere.
choices.consequence: False comfort ends the audit early.
choices.explanation: Absence from one database proves nothing about the rest.

blocks.debrief: The chain runs from exposure to a guessed or captured password, then to reuse, then to access. You cannot call back the first link, but a unique password stops the chain at reuse, and MFA and watchful session control make the later links harder. Replay any step you got wrong, then try the pattern on your own accounts.

blocks.title: Use the chain on another case

questions.prompt: A provider reports that only email addresses were exposed. What follows?

choices.text: Every password tied to that address must have leaked.
choices.explanation: An address on its own does not show that a password was exposed.

choices.text: Expect more targeted phishing, but no password leak has been established.
choices.explanation: The category of data matters. Check the provider’s own notice.

questions.prompt: When is a stolen password hash useful to an attacker?

choices.text: Sometimes it can be guessed offline, depending on the password and how it was hashed.
choices.explanation: A hash gives an attacker something to guess against, not the plaintext password.

choices.text: It always reveals the original password straight away.
choices.explanation: Hashing is not simple reversible encryption.

questions.prompt: Why should a reused password be changed at a second service as well?

choices.text: The second service’s database was copied along with the first.
choices.explanation: The danger is a login attempt with the same credentials, not a second copied database.

choices.text: The same pair may be tried there even though that service was never breached.
choices.explanation: Reuse carries the risk from one service to the next, which is how credential stuffing works.
